analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from rejecting renters using housing vouchers and penalizes neglected and warehoused vacant rental units.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced after its referral to three House committees in March 2023; it had no cosponsors and expired when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add 'source of income' to the Fair Housing Act, making it illegal nationwide for landlords to refuse renters who pay with Section 8 vouchers, Social Security, disability, or child support [S2] [S3]. It would fine owners $100,000 for deliberately letting a federally assisted unit fall below habitability standards, and $100,000 for every 30 days they intentionally leave a multifamily unit vacant beyond 60 days [S3]. It would also expand HUD complaint services for tenants, fund anti-harassment programs, and give landlords a tax credit for maintenance if they fix complaints quickly [S2] [S3]. It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor [S5] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who use federal rental assistance vouchers and other non-wage income. Voucher holders routinely report landlords refusing their subsidies, which keeps them locked out of apartments they can afford; a federal source-of-income ban, with penalties tenants can enforce in court, would give them the same Fair Housing Act protection as victims of race or sex discrimination [S3]. Tenants in multifamily buildings also gain complaint staffing, public disclosure of landlord complaints, and mandatory posting of tenant rights [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits discrimination based on source of income — including Section 8 vouchers, Social Security and disability benefits, and child support — across rental housing and real estate transactions, with penalties and private lawsuits for harmed tenants [S2] [S3].

Imposes a $100,000 civil penalty on owners who take actions intended to make a unit too rundown to qualify for HUD assistance, and lets affected tenants sue for $50,000 plus actual damages like the cost of finding a replacement home [S3].

Fines owners of federally assisted multifamily projects $100,000 for every 30 days a rental unit is intentionally left vacant beyond 60 days, aimed at owners who warehouse apartments rather than rent them [S3].

Requires HUD to staff its Multifamily Housing Complaint Line adequately, create a complaint resolution program for voucher tenants, publicly disclose landlord complaints, and require posting of tenant-rights notices in assisted buildings [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $25 million a year through 2028 for state, local, tribal, and nonprofit tenant harassment prevention programs, and roughly $140 million a year for fair housing enforcement and public education through 2033 [S3].

Gives landlords a tax credit equal to their maintenance expenses — up to $2,500 per low-income unit and $500,000 per taxpayer — if they resolve tenant complaints within 30 days, tying the subsidy to actual upkeep [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rental property owners, especially multifamily landlords with federally assisted or voucher-accepting buildings, bear new compliance duties, civil penalties, and exposure to tenant lawsuits. The public indirectly pays for the authorized spending and tax credits, which are not offset in the bill [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new costs on small and large landlords alike, and its vacancy and habitability penalties — $100,000 per violation — are severe enough that owners might avoid renting to voucher holders rather than accept the risk, unless enforcement is careful [S3].

The tax credit is not means-tested against landlord income and is funded through general tax revenue without offsets, so some of the benefit flows to landlords who would have maintained their buildings anyway [S3].

A national source-of-income ban overrides state and local landlord rules and pre-fills federal anti-discrimination obligations onto small independent owners, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voucher holders the upside is substantial: income-source discrimination is one of the main reasons vouchers go unused, and the bill pairs the ban with real penalties, enforcement funding, and a private right of action [S3]. The costs are real but bounded — penalties target intentional misconduct, repairs are presumed reasonable, and the landlord tax credit softens the maintenance burden. The main design risk is that heavy penalties could discourage some owners from participating in the voucher program at all, which the complaint-resolution and credit provisions only partly offset [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the Landlord Accountability Act of 2023 on March 7, 2023 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees; no committee took up the bill and no further action appears in its history [S5].
The bill never attracted a cosponsor, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill leaving committee [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and rental property owners are better off: they face no federal source-of-income discrimination ban, no penalties for degraded or warehoused assisted units, and no public disclosure of tenant complaints. Voucher holders remain without federal protection against being turned away for using their subsidy.

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it received no other sponsor or cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan breakdown of support ever appeared in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would impose a nationwide ban on rejecting voucher and benefit income, new penalties for degraded or warehoused units, and public disclosure of tenant complaints — real costs for owners. A maintenance tax credit up to $500,000 per taxpayer would offset some of that, but the industry's interest in the bill ran against the renters it regulates.

industries.industry: Tenant legal-aid and fair housing organizations
industries.note: The bill would authorize roughly $90 million a year for Fair Housing Initiatives Program groups, $47 million a year for state fair housing agencies, and $25 million a year for tenant harassment prevention programs, funding enforcement and legal help for tenants [S3].
